Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Zimbra Collaboration Suite below patched version 10.1.19 (Classic Web Client stored-XSS exposure)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Zimbra mailbox forwarding / Sieve filter rule created via web session (post-XSS session abuse) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Zimbra Collaboration Suite below patched version 10.1.19 (Classic Web Client stored-XSS exposure) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running Zimbra Collaboration Suite older than 10.1.19, the version that fixes the Classic Web Client stored-XSS that lets a crafted email run JavaScript in a victim's session. Because Zimbra assigned no CVE, TVM vuln feeds may miss it, so this hunts on software version directly. Rationale: Uses the article's exact concrete fixed version (Zimbra Collaboration Suite 10.1.19) as the version boundary; version-based hunt is needed because no CVE was assigned, so CVE-keyed TVM feeds under-report. High-fidelity because Zimbra version strings are unambiguous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/zimbra-urges-customers-to-patch-critical-web-client-xss-flaw/ • https://cyberpress.org/zimbra-10-1-19-fixes-stored-xss-flaw/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195130/hacking/update-now-critical-zimbra-classic-web-client-flaw-could-expose-mailboxes.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-27915
ATT&CKT1203
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentionally-retained lab/test Zimbra appliances kept on old builds for regression testing
  • TVM catalog lag briefly labeling a freshly-upgraded 10.1.19 host as still-vulnerable until next scan
  • Decommissioned Zimbra VMs still present in software inventory
  • Third-party Zimbra forks/derivatives whose version string parses below 10.1.19 but are separately patched
  • Hosts where only the modern (non-Classic) web client is enabled — flagged but not exploitable
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareName !has "test" and DeviceName !has "-lab"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a production Zimbra mailbox node and that the Classic Web Client is enabled (not only the modern client); verify SoftwareVersion is truly < 10.1.19 and not a mis-parsed build tag. 2) Contain: prioritize upgrade to ZCS 10.1.19 and reapply the SNMP mitigation if migrating from 10.0.x/9.0.x/8.8.15; where patching is delayed, disable the Classic Web Client or restrict external HTML/ICS rendering. 3) Hunt: on every vulnerable host, sweep for CVE-2025-27915-style exploitation — inbound emails with large/Base64 ICS content, and newly-created mailbox forwarding or Sieve filter rules (see companion UC).
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareVendor has_any ("zimbra","synacor") or SoftwareName has "zimbra"
| where SoftwareName has "zimbra" or SoftwareName has "collaboration"
| extend VerNum = extract(@"(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion)
| where isnotempty(VerNum) and parse_version(VerNum) < parse_version("10.1.19")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| sort by SoftwareVersion asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareVendor has_any ("zimbra","synacor") or SoftwareName has "zimbra"
| where SoftwareName has "zimbra" or SoftwareName has "collaboration"
| extend VerNum = extract(@"(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion)
| where isnotempty(VerNum) and parse_version(VerNum) < parse_version("10.1.19")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel

Zimbra mailbox forwarding / Sieve filter rule created via web session (post-XSS session abuse) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Zimbra mailbox/audit logs for creation of mail-forwarding addresses or Sieve filter rules — the documented post-exploitation action of the Classic Web Client stored-XSS family (CVE-2025-27915), where injected JavaScript in the victim's authenticated session silently redirects mail to attacker addresses. Excludes admin CLI (zmprov) changes to focus on web-session-originated modifications. Rationale: Grounded in genuine Zimbra LDAP/SOAP identifiers (zimbraPrefMailForwardingAddress, zimbraMailSieveScript, ModifyFilterRulesRequest) rather than invented strings; the mail-forwarding-rule outcome is the corroborated real-world impact of the actively-exploited sibling flaw CVE-2025-27915 (CISA KEV). Defender KQL left empty because Zimbra mailbox events do not land in Defender XDR tables. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/zimbra-zero-day-exploited-to-target.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-27915 • https://ccb.belgium.be/advisories/warning-stored-xss-vulnerability-zimbra-collaboration-web-client-actively-exploited
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1564.008
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately setting a personal-address auto-forward or vacation/out-of-office Sieve rule via preferences
  • Helpdesk configuring inbox filters on behalf of a user through the web client
  • Bulk provisioning of shared-mailbox forwarding during onboarding/migration
  • Mail-migration tooling importing Sieve scripts
  • Distribution-list or delegated-mailbox forwarding set up by mail admins through the web UI
Suppression filter
| where ExternalForward != "" and ExternalForward !endswith "@localhost" and SyslogMessage !has "zmprov"
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the forwarding target (ExternalForward) or Sieve body — is it an external/untrusted domain the user has no business forwarding to? Correlate the change time to an email the mailbox owner opened seconds earlier and to the user's normal client/geo. 2) Contain: delete the rogue forwarding address / filter rule, invalidate the user's active Zimbra sessions, and force a password reset. 3) Hunt: pivot on the external forward target across all mailboxes to find other victims, and search inbound mail for the triggering crafted message (large/Base64 ICS, HTML event handlers such as ontoggle in a <details> tag).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("zimbraPrefMailForwardingAddress","zimbraMailSieveScript","ModifyFilterRulesRequest","AddFilterRuleRequest")
| where SyslogMessage !has "zmprov"   // exclude admin CLI provisioning; XSS abuse comes via web/SOAP mailboxd
| extend ExternalForward = extract(@"zimbraPrefMailForwardingAddress=([^\s,;\]]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, ExternalForward, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Zimbra Mailbox Forwarding or Sieve Filter Change via Web Session
id: 8f3c1a94-2b7e-4d6a-9c1f-6b0e5a2d7f41
description: Detects creation/modification of Zimbra mail forwarding addresses or Sieve filter rules in mailbox/audit logs, the documented post-exploitation action of Classic Web Client stored-XSS (CVE-2025-27915 family). Excludes zmprov admin CLI activity.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-zimbra-flaw-could-let-crafted_0483473395.html
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-27915
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/12
tags:
  - attack.t1114.003
  - attack.t1564.008
logsource:
  product: linux
  service: syslog
detection:
  selection:
    - '|contains': 'zimbraPrefMailForwardingAddress'
    - '|contains': 'zimbraMailSieveScript'
    - '|contains': 'ModifyFilterRulesRequest'
    - '|contains': 'AddFilterRuleRequest'
  filter_admin:
    '|contains': 'zmprov'
  condition: selection and not filter_admin
level: medium
source:linux.syslog (zimbraPrefMailForwardingAddress OR zimbraMailSieveScript OR ModifyFilterRulesRequest OR AddFilterRuleRequest) -zmprov
APPLICATION
index=zimbra ("zimbraPrefMailForwardingAddress" OR "zimbraMailSieveScript" OR "ModifyFilterRulesRequest" OR "AddFilterRuleRequest") NOT "zmprov"
| rex field=_raw "zimbraPrefMailForwardingAddress=(?<external_forward>[^\s,;\]]+)"
| table _time host external_forward _raw
| sort - _time

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |

    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

date: 2026/05/02

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

DeviceFileEvents

| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] The Gentlemen internal reconnaissance via Advanced IP Scanner · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] GentleKiller BYOVD: ThrottleStop/ThrottleBlood driver load + All.exe/Allpatch2.exe EDR killer · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — No Manners Here: The Ruthless Rise of The Gentlemen Ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware scheduled task named 'gentlemen*' · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] The Gentlemen C2 / SystemBC egress to named attacker infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] The Gentlemen anti-forensics: wevtutil clearing Security/System event logs · [LLM] Pre-encryption Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic (The Gentlemen) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
The Gentlemen ransomware scheduled task named 'gentlemen*' AIInstallation High
Hunts creation, deletion, modification or execution of any Windows scheduled task whose name matches the string 'gentlemen', a signature Unit 42 explicitly attributes to The Gentlemen (Storm-2697) RaaS. This is the single highest-fidelity host artifact in the article because the actor-chosen task name is unique and not shared with any legitimate software. Rationale: Uses the article's literal, actor-attributed IOC (scheduled task matching 'gentlemen*') which Unit 42 recommends as a high-severity alert; corroborated as a Gentlemen RaaS artifact across ESET and Trend Micro write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal app or GPO that happens to include the substring 'gentlemen' in a task name (extremely rare)
  • Security tooling or a red-team engagement replaying Gentlemen TTPs for validation
  • A backup/monitoring vendor product name coincidentally containing the token
  • An analyst manually recreating the task during IR to study it
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Windows\\System32\\GroupPolicy\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full task XML/action (schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml) and the InitiatingProcess command line — confirm the task executes an attacker binary rather than a benign path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable/delete the task, and suspend the executing account; snapshot for forensics before deletion. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same task name, and pivot to BYOVD driver loads (ThrottleBlood.sys), wevtutil log clears, and shadow-copy deletion on the same devices to scope encryption readiness.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("ScheduledTask","gentlemen"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "gentlemen")
    or (EventID in (4698,4699,4700,4701,4702) and EventData has "gentlemen")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, EventID, NewProcessName, CommandLine, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GentleKiller BYOVD: ThrottleStop/ThrottleBlood driver load + All.exe/Allpatch2.exe EDR killer AIExploitation High
Hunts The Gentlemen's GentleKiller EDR-killer framework: kernel load of the vulnerable ThrottleStop.sys driver (or its attacker-renamed variant ThrottleBlood.sys) abusing CVE-2025-7771, and execution of the All.exe/Allpatch2.exe killer binaries that terminate 400+ security processes. Article-specific because it names the exact driver and CVE; the renamed driver and killer binaries are confirmed by Trend Micro and DarkReading. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named CVE-2025-7771 / ThrottleStop.sys driver plus the externally-confirmed renamed ThrottleBlood.sys and All.exe/Allpatch2.exe killer binaries — all Gentlemen-unique, so very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/gentlemen-ransomware-vulnerable-driver-security-gear • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine ThrottleStop CPU-undervolting utility loading throttlestop.sys on an enthusiast/OC workstation (filtered by requiring killer-parent or the renamed driver)
  • Driver testing by a hardware/BIOS team in a lab
  • An unrelated internal tool coincidentally named all.exe (validate publisher/signing)
  • Security-vendor driver-block validation replaying the vulnerable driver
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "throttlestop.sys" and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "throttlestop.exe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "ThrottleStop")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the loaded driver is ThrottleBlood.sys (always malicious) or ThrottleStop.sys loaded by all.exe/allpatch2.exe/rundll32; check whether EDR sensors on the host went silent immediately after. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the driver hash via ASR/WDAC and the killer binary hashes, and force EDR tamper-protection re-enable. 3) Hunt: identify which security processes were terminated, then look for follow-on shadow-copy deletion and encryption; sweep for the same driver/killer hashes fleet-wide.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("throttleblood.sys","throttlestop.sys")
| where FileName =~ "throttleblood.sys" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("all.exe","allpatch2.exe","rundll32.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\All.exe","\\Allpatch2.exe") or CommandLine has_any ("ThrottleBlood.sys","ThrottleStop.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen anti-forensics: wevtutil clearing Security/System event logs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts use of wevtutil (or PowerShell Clear-EventLog) to clear the Security or System logs, a defense-evasion step Unit 42 explicitly ties to The Gentlemen and recommends behavioral alerting on. Pairs the LOLBin with the specific target logs to keep fidelity high. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit recommendation to alert on wevtutil clearing Security/System logs; the LOLBin+target-log pairing keeps it far above bare-wevtutil noise. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://redpiranha.net/news/the-gentlemen-ransomware-analysis
ATT&CKT1070.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin or SCCM script clearing logs during routine maintenance/re-imaging
  • Log-forwarding troubleshooting that rotates/clears channels
  • A monitoring agent rolling event logs
  • Forensic tooling that clears after export
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe") and AccountName !in~ ("system")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the account and parent process behind wevtutil; benign clears are usually SYSTEM/GPO, attacker clears often follow EDR-kill or come from an interactive/RDP session. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve any surviving logs and forwarded copies, and suspend the account. 3) Hunt: because logs were wiped, pivot to forwarded/SIEM copies and correlate with GentleKiller driver loads, scheduled-task 'gentlemen', and shadow-copy deletion to reconstruct the timeline.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Security","System"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Clear-EventLog")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 1102 | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, Signal="SecurityLogCleared_1102", CommandLine=""),
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "wevtutil.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log") and CommandLine has_any ("Security","System") | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, Signal="wevtutil_clear", CommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Ransomware Event Log Clearing via wevtutil
id: c4e2f9a1-77b3-4a2c-8e19-5d6b0a3f1c88
description: Detects clearing of the Windows Security or System event logs via wevtutil, a defense-evasion step attributed to The Gentlemen RaaS.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/12
tags:
  - attack.t1070.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\wevtutil.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'cl '
      - 'clear-log'
  targets:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'Security'
      - 'System'
  condition: selection and targets
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\wevtutil.exe OR *\WEVTUTIL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*"cl "* OR *clear-log* OR *Clear-Log*) @CommandLine:(*Security* OR *System*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\wevtutil\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\b(cl|clear-log)\b/i
| CommandLine=/(Security|System)/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=wevtutil.exe AND (Processes.process="*cl *" OR Processes.process="*clear-log*") AND (Processes.process="*Security*" OR Processes.process="*System*")) OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Clear-EventLog*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where user!="*$"
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=wevtutil.exe AND (Processes.process="*cl *" OR Processes.process="*clear-log*") AND (Processes.process="*Security*" OR Processes.process="*System*")) OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Clear-EventLog*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where user!="*$"
| sort - lastTime
Pre-encryption Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic (The Gentlemen) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts destruction of Volume Shadow Copies with vssadmin or wmic immediately before encryption — the article's named impact-phase behavior for The Gentlemen. Restricts to the specific delete verbs to keep it a genuine ransomware precursor rather than a snapshot-lifecycle dashboard. Rationale: Directly implements the article's impact-phase recommendation (behavioral alert on vssadmin/wmic shadow-copy deletion); verb-scoped to avoid benign snapshot lifecycle. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://redpiranha.net/news/the-gentlemen-ransomware-analysis
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/other backup software pre-snapshot cleanup calling vssadmin delete
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting VSS/DISM disk-cleanup operations
  • Disk-provisioning or golden-image build scripts pruning shadows
  • Application installers that reset shadow storage
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","beremote.exe","vsnapvss.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("services.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the parent process and account — backup software/SYSTEM under a service parent is likely benign; an interactive shell or a parent tied to GentleKiller is not. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately (encryption is imminent), kill the process tree, and disable the account. 3) Hunt: look for concurrent mass file writes/rename-to-new-extension, the 'gentlemen' scheduled task, and BYOVD driver loads on the same and neighboring hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
    or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has "delete" and CommandLine has "shadows")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "shadowcopy" and CommandLine has "delete")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Ransomware Shadow Copy Deletion (vssadmin/wmic)
id: d7a3c1e9-6b48-4f2a-91c7-8e0d5a2b3f16
description: Detects Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin or wmic, the article-named pre-encryption impact step for The Gentlemen RaaS.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/12
tags:
  - attack.t1490
  - attack.impact
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  vssadmin:
    Image|endswith: '\vssadmin.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'delete'
      - 'shadows'
  wmic:
    Image|endswith: '\wmic.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'shadowcopy'
      - 'delete'
  condition: vssadmin or wmic
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 ((@Image:(*\vssadmin.exe OR *\VSSADMIN.EXE) @CommandLine:(*delete* OR *Delete*) @CommandLine:(*shadows* OR *Shadows*)) OR (@Image:(*\wmic.exe OR *\WMIC.EXE) @CommandLine:(*shadowcopy* OR *ShadowCopy*) @CommandLine:(*delete* OR *Delete*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\vssadmin\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/delete/i AND CommandLine=/shadows/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\wmic\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/shadowcopy/i AND CommandLine=/delete/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name=vssadmin.exe AND Processes.process="*delete*" AND Processes.process="*shadows*") OR (Processes.process_name=wmic.exe AND Processes.process="*shadowcopy*" AND Processes.process="*delete*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where user!="*$"
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name=vssadmin.exe AND Processes.process="*delete*" AND Processes.process="*shadows*") OR (Processes.process_name=wmic.exe AND Processes.process="*shadowcopy*" AND Processes.process="*delete*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where user!="*$"
| sort - lastTime
The Gentlemen internal reconnaissance via Advanced IP Scanner AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts execution of Advanced IP Scanner (including renamed copies) which Unit 42 states The Gentlemen frequently uses for internal network mapping before lateral movement. Matches on the product/company metadata so renamed binaries are still caught. Rationale: Uses the article's named recon tool (Advanced IP Scanner) with Famatech/product-name metadata matching so renamed drops still fire; hunting tier because the tool has legitimate IT-admin use. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://www.cryptika.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware-with-custom-edr-av-killers-scaling-faster-to-attack-industries-worldwide/
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT/helpdesk staff using Advanced IP Scanner for inventory
  • MSP or network engineer performing an authorized sweep
  • Vulnerability-management onboarding scan
  • Renamed portable copy carried on a technician's USB toolkit
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("svc_netscan","helpdesk_admin")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the executing account is IT/admin on a jump host (likely benign) or a compromised user/host with no admin role and off-hours timing. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host and suspend the account before lateral movement. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for follow-on SMB/RDP/SSH connections to newly-discovered hosts, PsExec/wmic remote exec, and GentleKiller/encryption precursors.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("advanced_ip_scanner.exe","advanced_port_scanner.exe")
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Advanced IP Scanner"
    or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Famatech"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "advanced_ip_scanner.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "advanced_port_scanner.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Recon Tool - Advanced IP Scanner Execution
id: e9b4d2a7-1c53-4d6f-8a20-3f7e9b1c5a44

The Gentlemen C2 / SystemBC egress to named attacker infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from endpoints to the three IPs bundled with the article's Gentlemen IOC set, associated with SystemBC SOCKS5 C2 the group uses for command-and-control. Surfaces the initiating process so an analyst can confirm whether a LOLBin or the SystemBC proxy is beaconing. Rationale: Uses the three C2 IPs from the article's IOC bundle tied to SystemBC; kept at hunting/Medium because these specific IPs were not independently corroborated by my two external searches (which confirmed SystemBC usage but not the IPs) — analysts should validate against current threat-intel before promoting to alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/
ATT&CKT1090 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The IP is reassigned/sinkholed and later hosts a benign service (IOC decay)
  • A shared-hosting IP that also serves legitimate content
  • Security researcher/VPN egress coincidentally hitting the address
  • Threat-intel scanner or honeypot traffic in your own range
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — SystemBC often runs as an unsigned binary from temp/appdata or a LOLBin proxy; confirm the connection is beaconing (periodic, non-standard port) not a one-off. 2) Contain: block the IPs at the firewall/EDR, isolate the beaconing host, and capture the process binary. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process hash fleet-wide, check for Cloudflare-tunnel/AnyDesk persistence, and correlate with GentleKiller and shadow-copy deletion to gauge encryption readiness.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","45.86.230.112")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","45.86.230.112")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2025-7771", "CVE-2023-27532", "CVE-2024-37085")

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0d
status: experimental
description: |
    schtasks.exe /create with payload-shaped action — points at
    powershell, cmd, rundll32, encoded-base64, or user-writable paths.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
author: Clankerusecase

    - attack.t1053.005
    - attack.persistence

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_schtasks:

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"

    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — No Manners Here: The Ruthless Rise of The Gentlemen Ransomware Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — No Manners Here: The Ruthless Rise of The Gentlemen Ransomware
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("throttlestop.sys"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("throttlestop.sys"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,

TSDProxy management-API replay via injected x-tsdproxy-auth-token to loopback :8080 AIExploitation High
Hunts a backend-resident process replaying the leaked internal TSDProxy auth token to the localhost management API (127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1) with a spoofed x-tsdproxy-id, bypassing Tailscale auth to gain admin control. Article-specific because it keys on the exact forwarded header names and the loopback management endpoint. Rationale: Keys on the exact leaked-header names (x-tsdproxy-auth-token / x-tsdproxy-id) plus the loopback management endpoint (127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1) from the PoC — both are near-unique strings, so a match is almost certainly the token-replay attack. Cross-checked GitLab GLAD and cvereports for endpoint/port confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TSDProxy maintainer/QA running the documented PoC or a regression test that replays the token
  • Security team validating the patch by reproducing the exploit in a lab
  • Home-lab admin manually curling the management API with sample headers copied from the advisory
  • Automated integration test harness for tsdproxy that exercises /api/v1 with identity headers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tsdproxy") and AccountName !in~ ("tsdproxy")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/container and confirm it is NOT the tsdproxy binary itself; pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the x-tsdproxy-id value used. 2) Contain: isolate the host/container, rotate the TSDProxy process auth token (restart tsdproxy) and set identityHeaders:false, then upgrade to >=1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e. 3) Hunt: review /api/v1 access for proxy start/stop/pause and webhook-trigger calls (SSRF), enumerate which backends received the forwarded token, and check for prior /debug/headers-style token-capture requests on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents

ImProcessCreate

Unexpected process connecting to TSDProxy loopback management port 127.0.0.1:8080 AIExploitation Medium
Network-shape variant that catches token replay performed with an HTTP library (python-requests, node, Go) where the header strings never hit a command line. Flags non-tsdproxy processes opening a loopback connection to the management port :8080, the interface the advisory says the management API binds to. Rationale: Catches the replay when the token is sent via an HTTP library (no header string in the cmdline) by pivoting on the loopback management port (:8080) named in the advisory, scoped to interpreter/CLI processes and excluding tsdproxy itself. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/
ATT&CKT1550.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Another local web service (many apps default to :8080) being probed by curl during ops work
  • Container init/entrypoint scripts curling a co-located backend that also listens on 8080
  • Developer testing an API on localhost:8080 unrelated to tsdproxy

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("x-tsdproxy-auth-token","x-tsdproxy-id","/api/v1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination :8080 process is the tsdproxy management server (not another app) and identify the connecting process and its container. 2) Contain: if the caller is an untrusted backend, isolate it, restart tsdproxy to rotate the token, and set identityHeaders:false. 3) Hunt: correlate the same source process with process-creation events for x-tsdproxy-auth-token strings (UC1) and review /api/v1 write operations that followed the connection.

TSDProxy forwarded-token harvesting via header-reflection endpoint or header grep AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-access step where an attacker with backend code execution extracts the forwarded x-tsdproxy-auth-token — e.g. curling a header-reflection route (/debug/headers) and parsing the token out, or grepping/jq-ing it from request headers/logs. Article-specific because it keys on the exact header name and the PoC's reflection-endpoint capture technique. Rationale: Targets the PoC's token-capture step: fetching /debug/headers and parsing X-Tsdproxy-Auth-Token, or grepping/jq-ing the unique header name — distinct pivot from the replay (excludes 127.0.0.1:8080//api/v1 to avoid overlap with UC1). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/
ATT&CKT1528

Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and the process/container; determine whether the token value was written to a file or piped onward. 2) Contain: treat the token as compromised — restart tsdproxy to rotate it, set identityHeaders:false, and upgrade to the fixed pseudo-version 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host for a subsequent replay to 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1 (UC1/UC2) and review webhook/proxy config enumeration that would follow successful admin access.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","/api/v1"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

Surfaces hosts/containers running TSDProxy so the SOC can confirm the version is below the fixed Go pseudo-version 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e and that identityHeaders is not set to false. SiYuan Electron renderer spawns shell/LOLBin (stored-XSS-to-RCE via nodeIntegration) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE stage of CVE-2026-50551/CVE-2026-54158: a stored XSS payload in an attribute-view cell fires in SiYuan's Electron renderer, which runs with nodeIntegration:true and reaches require('child_process') to spawn arbitrary host commands. SiYuan is a note-taking app and should never parent cmd/powershell/wscript, so any such child is high-fidelity RCE. Rationale: Uses the exact article-named parent binary (SiYuan.exe) and the nodeIntegration→child_process RCE chain; a knowledge-management Electron app spawning interpreters is near-zero baseline, making the parent→child pair high-fidelity. Cross-checked GitLab Advisory DB (CVE-2026-54158) and the SiYuan GitHub security advisories confirming the same nodeIntegration:true/contextIsolation:false config across the CVE family. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54158/ • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-50551/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.007 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan community plugins that legitimately shell out (e.g. export-to-PDF, git-sync, or pandoc integration plugins invoking node/cmd)
  • Developers running SiYuan from source spawning node.exe during build/watch
  • SiYuan auto-updater launching a helper/installer process on version upgrade
  • Security tooling injecting into or wrapping SiYuan.exe and inheriting the parent name
  • conhost.exe host allocation appearing as a benign child on interpreter launch
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "conhost.exe") | where not (FileName =~ "node.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--build","electron","webpack"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and grandchild tree on the host; benign plugin activity has recognisable args (pandoc, git, node build), whereas RCE shows encoded PowerShell, downloaders, or discovery commands. Confirm SiYuan version < 3.7.0 (vulnerable). 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the SiYuan process tree, and quarantine the user's workspace `data/storage/av/*.json` files before they re-sync to other devices. 3) Hunt: enumerate every device sharing that user's SiYuan sync/workspace (this bug fires on every peer that opens the poisoned row), review those hosts for the same SiYuan.exe child-process pattern and any outbound C2 from the spawned child.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SiYuan.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","node.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\SiYuan.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe",@"\powershell.exe",@"\pwsh.exe",@"\wscript.exe",@"\cscript.exe",@"\mshta.exe",@"\rundll32.exe",@"\regsvr32.exe",@"\certutil.exe",@"\bitsadmin.exe",@"\curl.exe",@"\node.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Out-of-band write to SiYuan attribute-view store (data/storage/av/*.json payload plant) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the persistence/plant stage of CVE-2026-50551: the malicious attribute-view cell is written to data/storage/av/<avID>.json and rides workspace sync to every peer. A process other than SiYuan.exe writing to that exact store path indicates manual/malware staging of the payload or an external sync client propagating a poisoned AV file. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact backing-store path data/storage/av/<avID>.json plus the fact that only SiYuan.exe should author those files; a foreign writer surfaces manual PoC-style plants and malware staging the poisoned AV JSON. Corroborated against the SiYuan GitHub advisory and GitLab Advisory DB confirming the storage path and sync-propagation model. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54158/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-50551/
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party sync clients (Dropbox.exe, OneDrive.exe, Syncthing.exe, Resilio) writing the workspace JSON — note these are ALSO the legitimate payload-propagation vector, so triage rather than blanket-exclude
  • Backup/restore software (Veeam, Duplicati, robocopy) copying the workspace into place
  • User manually restoring a workspace snapshot or migrating between machines
  • Antivirus/EDR remediation rewriting the file after a scan
  • Text editors or scripts a power-user runs to bulk-edit their own SiYuan database
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe","Syncthing.exe","ResilioSync.exe","robocopy.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve the written data/storage/av/*.json and grep the cell content for HTML breakout patterns (</textarea>, "><img, src=x, onerror=, <script); a benign SiYuan AV file contains none. Identify the writing process — if it is a sync client, treat as propagation and pivot to origin. 2) Contain: quarantine the offending JSON, block the SiYuan sync channel for the affected workspace, and prevent peers from opening the block-attribute panel until cleaned. 3) Hunt: on every device sharing that workspace, look for the paired RCE signal (UC: SiYuan.exe spawning cmd/powershell/node) and confirm all endpoints are upgraded to SiYuan >= 3.7.0.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where FileName endswith ".json"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("SiYuan.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".json"
| where ActingProcessName !has "SiYuan.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File Browser hook-auth pre-auth RCE: filebrowser spawns shell/recon commands (CVE-2026-54088) AIExploitation High
Hunts the File Browser server binary (`filebrowser`) spawning a shell or OS discovery/tooling child process. Under CVE-2026-54088 an unauthenticated attacker injects shell metacharacters into the login username/password, which `os.Expand` substitutes unsanitised into the admin's hook-auth command, causing the `filebrowser` process to execute attacker OS commands. A file server should essentially never spawn `id`/`whoami`/`curl`/`wget`, so any such child is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the concrete vulnerable binary name `filebrowser` (parent) plus the article's PoC injection primitive (shell metacharacters `;`/`$(`/backtick and `id`/`whoami` running under the hook command). A file-server process spawning recon/OS tooling is near-zero in benign operation. Cross-checked against filebrowser.org auth docs and auth/hook.go on GitHub. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1033 T1087.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately configured a hook-auth command that shells out to an external auth backend using curl/wget (e.g. validating against an LDAP/OIDC gateway)
  • Custom container entrypoint or healthcheck wrapper also named 'filebrowser' spawning /bin/sh for readiness probes
  • Ops running the filebrowser CLI (`filebrowser config`, `filebrowser users`) interactively from a shell where the parent/child order is inverted
  • Backup/maintenance scripts invoked by a filebrowser-named systemd unit that call uname/hostname
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^\s*test\s" and not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alert — confirm InitiatingProcessFileName=='filebrowser' and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for injected recon (id/whoami/cat /etc/passwd) or separators; correlate to the host's web/reverse-proxy logs for a POST to /api/login in the same second. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the filebrowser container/service, and disable hook authentication (set auth.method back to json/proxy) or patch to filebrowser v2 > 2.63.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for follow-on egress/reverse shells (UC2), new files under the served directory (webshell/backdoor), new cron entries or SSH authorized_keys, and any outbound connection from the filebrowser process subtree.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where (FileName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php"))
    or (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh")
        and (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where (TargetProcessName has_any ("/id","/whoami","/uname","/hostname","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/perl","/ruby","/php"))
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh")
        and (TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  tool_child:

level: high
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^filebrowser$/i
| (ImageFileName=/\/(id|whoami|uname|hostname|curl|wget|nc|ncat|socat|python[0-9]?|perl|ruby|php)$/i OR (ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|ash|zsh|ksh)$/i AND regex("(/etc/passwd|/etc/shadow|whoami|uname|/dev/tcp/|;|\\$\\()", field=CommandLine)))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
